The Outlook for Cobalt 2012 # Executive Summary What will happen to the market surplus? - The cobalt market is currently being impacted by oversupply and slower than expected demand. Prices of low grade material contracted by 12.3% year-on-year to US$16.44/lb in 2011 and a further 18.5% year-on-year to US$14.43/lb in H1 2012. CRU forecasts that prices will average US$14.00/lb in full year 2012 due to a combination of refined surplus along with high levels of inventories of raw materials in China. Looking ahead, we predict that consecutive annual surpluses in the refined market will continue weighing on prices in the medium-term. It is anticipated that prices will reach a low of US$12.80/lb in 2014, before increasing to US$17.00/lb in 2017, when the refined market is predicted to turn to a deficit. - Despite a slower than expected consumption growth in the near-term, we anticipate that demand for refined cobalt will register a CAGR of 6.1% in 2000-2022. This is largely driven by demand for cobalt oxide used in rechargeable batteries. Other sectors such as aerospace and advanced engineering are projected to support robust demand growth. Indeed, cobalt demand patterns are partly a function of advances in new technology and developments in traditional metallurgical sectors. The use of cobalt by growing and high value added end-use sectors does not mean that this commodity is unaffected by a weaker economic outlook. - In addition to rapidly growing volumes, the supply side of the cobalt market has recently become more complicated as an increasing amount of concentrates and intermediates are produced and used as feed in the production of refined material, in particular chemicals. CRU estimates that, currently, about 60% of total cobalt units come from mines in the African Copper Belt. Production of intermediate products is registering considerable growth and will be the preferred raw material of refined producers due to higher cobalt content, compared to concentrates, and operational efficiency. nt in the cobalt market is one characterised by oversupply concerns. Even though demand has been expanding at a CAGR of 6.0% in the last 10 years, capacity additions mainly triggered by copper and nickel projects have added a significant amount of cobalt units, thus putting downward pressure on prices. The above, coupled with macroeconomic challenges, generates a bearish feeling in the cobalt market. Since mid-2011, this negative feeling has been exacerbated by a slowdown in China; nevertheless, cobalt consumption is growing strongly but at a slower rate than projected last year. Benchmark 99.3% prices contracted by 12.3% to US$16.44/lb in 2011. In H1 2012, prices registered further losses to US$14.43/lb, an 18.5% decline from H1 2011. CRU forecasts that prices will average US$14.00/lb in 2012; at the time of writing, 99.3% material was trading below US$13.00/lb. Oversupply concerns have been weighing on prices. We estimate that the refined cobalt market was balanced in 2010 and exhibited a surplus of 2,781 tonnes in 2011. For the current year, we predict that the surplus will fall to 420 tonnes. This is mainly attributed to the fact that small Chinese processors are expected to cut primary production in the current year. However, the predicted fall in the market surplus for 2012 does not imply that the cobalt market will be tighter. This is because there is a significant accumulation of concentrates and intermediates stocks; we estimate that those stocks in China amount to about 17,000 tonnes of cobalt contained. We believe that the raw material stockpile in China is another factor putting downward pressure on market prices. Those inventories are expected to fall in order to meet a deficit in the raw material market in 2011-2013. In addition, there is evidence from trade statistics that Chinese imports of cobalt feed have recently fallen substantially. While it is more obvious to assess market tightness by looking at the refined market balance, CRU is of the opinion that the cobalt raw material market also has an important role. This is especially relevant for by-products, as mine output does not necessarily respond to the needs of the final market. ### Oversupply has been putting pressure on prices since 2010 US$/lb

CRU International Limited confidential The Outlook for Cobalt 2012 Executive Summary 3 ### Future market: Supply shortages are expected in the long-term The current oversupply concerns extend to the medium-term as well. While refined demand is anticipated to expand at a CAGR of 6.8% in 2012-2017, supply growth is expected to be faster. Taking a conservative approach in our supply forecasts, we predict that the refined cobal

t market will see consecutive annual surpluses in 2013-2016.  We believe that the refined market surplus will reach 4,173 tonnes in 2014; benchmark prices are predicted to contract to US$12.80/lb in that year.  The refined market is projected to turn to a deficit in 2017; prices are forecast to increase to US$17.00/lb. 

CRU would like to emphasise the fact that our refined production forecasts are backed by sufficient supply of raw materials.  Our detailed raw material supply projection out to 2017 shows that there will be sufficient feed to support refined production.  In fact, due to significant capacity additions of intermediate products, total raw material supply growth is expected to be enough in order to meet refined production needs out to 2017.  CRU believes that raw material supply growth will be mainly a result of robust growth in the supply of intermediate products, rather than concentrates.  It is anticipated that the supply of concentrates will fall.  The DRC intends to process concentrates domestically, in order to capture the value added and export feed in the form of intermediates.  This trend is justified by recent trade statistics and CRU believes that it will continue in the medium-term. 

However, the cobalt market is anticipated to see a turning point in the long-run.  With demand expected to continue growing robustly, we believe that there is going to be a shortage of cobalt units. Even though in the near/medium-term the cobalt market is expected to be oversupplied mainly due to significant copper/nickel-triggered capacity additions, the picture changes dramatically in the longterm.  Looking at the potential of new projects, we understand that the outlook for further additions is uncertain.  From what we identify as active new projects, 75% of them are still at the exploration and development stage.  Medium-term oversupply concerns and low current prices have affected the development of new projects.  This has also been impacted by a weak macroeconomic environment. 

A long-term shortage of cobalt units is based on the prediction that refined demand will have grown at a CAGR of 6.1% in 2000-2022.  This growth rate is largely a function of consumption trends, especially in the critical field of rechargeable batteries.  As the size of the total cobalt market grows, the additional quantity demanded each year by end-use sectors increases as well.  For instance, in the period 2001-2010, demand for refined cobalt grew at an average of 3,228 tonnes per annum. However, according to CRU’s projections the equivalent volume in 2011-2020 is anticipated to soar to 6,021 tonnes.  In practice this is about the size of one project alone.  New capacity may come from a variety of operations; importantly, the sources of finance as well as the degree of risk aversion for each project can vary significantly.  The above factors will drive the long-term price of cobalt.

That was a return to long-term growth rates, down from a 13.9% expansion in 2010. Our estimates suggest that cobalt demand growth is strong and consistently outperforms advances in the global industrial production index. Demand from chemical sectors reached 44,150 tonnes in 2011, a 6.3% increase from the previous year. That was primarily driven by cobalt oxide used in lithium ion battery cells. It was also supported by demand for cobalt oxide, which is used in the manufacture of PET. CRU introduced a new end-use sector for cobalt sulphate; we identified that copper production used 471 tonnes of cobalt contained in 2011. Demand from metallurgical sectors rose by 5.3% year-on-year to 32,865 tonnes in 2011. Cobalt used in cemented carbides and rotating components for aircraft engines saw strong growth, boosted by healthy demand from the engineering and aerospace sectors respectively. It is anticipated that refined cobalt consumption will increase by 5.9% year-on-year to 81,554 tonnes in 2012. Despite a weaker than previously expected economic outlook, CRU believes that demand for cobalt will benefit from high value added and growing end-use sectors. Expanding markets such as batteries for high-end electronic devices and EV/HEV, the aerospace industry, and advanced engineering are projected to keep fuelling the strong demand momentum in the short/medium and long-term. Our consumption forecasts suggest that refined cobalt demand will register a CAGR of 6.1% in 2000-2022, reaching 149,423 tonnes by 2022. Long-term consumption trends show that the Asian cobalt consumption share is expanding rapidly. Considering that Asian demand growth is mainly driven by chemical consumption, we believe that Asia, in particular China, is gaining the new cobalt market share established by cutting-edge technologies. Traditional metallurgical sectors are predicted to maintain a considerable share in industrialised regions; however, this is gradually growing in developing regions too, supported by supply chain trends of end-use sectors, production migration, and transfer of technology. ## Cobalt demand exhibits a robust long-term growth pattern tonnes

CRU estimates that mine production amounted to 97,003 tonnes cobalt contained in 2011, 60% of which originated from the African Copper Belt. A total of 14 identified operations in the DRC produced ore and concentrate, most of which was exported as feed. Production of intermediate products totalled 35,456 tonnes in 2011; we expect that production of cobalt intermediates will reach 69,230 tonnes by 2017, replacing concentrate as feed in refined cobalt production. Major nickel and copper operations that do not produce refined cobalt metal will contribute to that growth. Intermediates will be the raw material of choice for refined producers due to higher cobalt content than concentrates, as well as logistical and processing efficiency. Total refined supply reached 79,796 tonnes in 2011, twice as high the level in 2000. Chemical products totalled 45,476 tonnes in 2011, primarily using cobalt units from the DRC. Production of refined chemicals is dominated by OMG, Chinese processors and the Yabulu refinery. We believe that small Chinese processors are cutting production in 2012, impacted by low prices and a demand slowdown. Looking ahead, it is anticipated that large-scale refiners will capture that loss, benefiting from lower processing costs. CRU projects that refined supply will amount to 111,867 tonnes by 2017; secondary cobalt supply from recycling (Umicore) is expected to gain momentum. This year, we present our production cost estimates based on the specific costs of producing cobalt. Half of forecast cobalt production in 2017 will be produced at around US$3.0/lb or below. This will come from nickel refineries and integrated metal producers. A considerable refined volume will be produced in the form of hydrometallurgical intermediates, at a cost of US$5.0-8.0/lb. At operations where cobalt is produced as a main product, costs will be in the range of US$9.0-15.0/lb. The top of the cost curve will be formed by refined chemical producers in China. Indeed, Chinese processors that mainly use purchased hydrometallurgical intermediates as their feed will see costs of US$16.4020.80/lb, due to high-cost raw materials. The Outlook for Cobalt 2012     Executive Summary 

### Upside risks to the price outlook 

**Stronger than anticipated industrial and economic outlook.** A stronger than expected industrial production activity will favour cobalt consumption.  That will support several end-uses that consume superalloys.  However, given the current economic outlook, the risks are mainly on the downside.  A stronger than expected world economic activity will accelerate urbanisation trends, thus boosting the markets for high-end electronics and air travel. 

**Favourable end-use technology developments that require a higher cobalt intensity of use.** Examples include the emergence of tablets or a potential new end-use sector consuming rechargeable batteries; interestingly, robust growth of mobile phones and laptops significantly boosted cobalt consumption over the last 10 years. 

**Delays in the start-up or ramp-up of new cobalt metal projects.** New projects are always subject to operational and financial setbacks, even shortly before commissioning.   Especially the projects located in higher risk regions may be subject to longer delays.  Despite the fact that CRU has been conservative in our forecasts, delays are always possible. 

**Technical challenges at HPAL operations.** There has been evidence that major HPAL operations are successfully commissioning.  However, this kind of operations has historically experienced technical challenges that should not be disregarded when conducting a high and low case scenario analysis. 

### Downside risks to the price outlook 

**Weaker than anticipated industrial production activity.** Considering the advanced level of downside macroeconomic risks, especially in industrialised countries, deterioratio

n in industrial activity will have an impact on cobalt consumption. For instance, a weaker than expected world industrial activity will affect the market for cemented carbides as demand from the automotive, steel and shipbuilding industries will soften. #### **Unfavourable technology developments that trigger substitution of cobalt or lower intensity of** **use.** Miniaturisation trends in end-use markets will affect cobalt consumption. This is very important in high-end devices that need to be lighter and smaller over time. The most critical end-use sector is lithium ion rechargeable batteries. **Refined cobalt production stronger compared to CRU’s expectations.** CRU has taken a conservative approach to forecasting refined cobalt production. If the actual production level is higher than what we project, the refined cobalt market will exhibit a higher surplus. Our conservative forecasting approach applies both to large and small scale operations. **Aggressive development of new projects.** If that takes place it will affect mainly the long-run outlook, considering the time needed to develop new projects. Lately, in view of the growing consumption volume of cobalt, as well as its contribution to high-end technologies, there has been a growing interest from investment groups to be involved in the cobalt industry.
